Hatchlings of the Sandhill crane (Antigone canadensis) emerge at a wet weight of 109.1 grams [Wwb = 109.1 grams], a modest mass that reflects the caloric constraints of yolk provisioning in a large-bodied precocial species. Eggs incubated at a consistent temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C] produce chicks after an incubation period of 26.7 days [ab = 26.7 days]. This duration is comparable to that of other large gruids and represents a trade-off between protecting the developing embryo and minimizing the window of vulnerability to nest predators. Upon hatching, the downy young are capable of leaving the nest within hours, though they remain dependent on their parents for thermoregulation and food delivery during the first critical days. Field researchers have noted that the neonatal mass is a strong predictor of early survival, as heavier chicks are better able to withstand periods of inclement weather and food scarcity common in the prairie breeding grounds.

As the young Sandhill crane enters its first weeks of life, the transition to independent locomotion is marked by the achievement of fledging. Under the thermal regime typical of active metabolic periods in this species, which centers around 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], the time since birth at fledging is recorded at 38.6 days since birth [tx = 38.6 days since birth]. This relatively rapid development of flight capability from hatching is characteristic of precocial birds that must escape terrestrial predators. The fledgling's initial flights are short and awkward, but within a week, the young bird gains sufficient coordination to travel several hundred meters. This milestone is crucial for dispersal from the nesting territory, which reduces intraspecific competition for food resources concentrated near the nest site. Senior ornithologists have noted that cranes hatched later in the season exhibit a slightly protracted fledging interval, likely due to lower ambient temperatures affecting arthropod prey availability.

The prolonged period between fledging and the attainment of full reproductive capability is a defining feature of Sandhill crane life history. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at approximately 115.8 days from birth [tp = approximately 115.8 days from birth], calculated under the species' typical active body temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This timing represents a significant physiological milestone, as the juvenile skeleton must be nearly fully ossified to support the energetic demands of courtship displays and eventual egg production. Following puberty, individuals do not breed immediately; instead, they undergo a protracted period of social learning, often forming pair bonds that last several years before their first successful nesting attempt. The delay between sexual maturation and first reproduction is common among long-lived birds and is thought to allow young cranes to refine foraging skills and establish stable territories.

Reproductive investment in the Sandhill crane is characterized by a modest annual output, consistent with their K-selected life-history strategy. Females typically lay a single clutch containing 1 egg per breeding attempt [N_R_i = 1 egg per breeding attempt], and they produce 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2 clutches per year]. The first successful brood is initiated at 1095 days after birth [tR = 1095 days after birth], a value recorded under thermal conditions of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This protracted pre-reproductive period is among the longest recorded for any North American bird of comparable body mass and reflects the complexity of crane social structure, including elaborate pair-bonding rituals and the defense of large, multipurpose territories. The selective advantage of this delayed first reproduction likely lies in the high survival probability of adults, which offsets the low annual fecundity.

Adult Sandhill cranes achieve an ultimate wet weight of 4110 grams [Wwi = 4110 grams] on average, with males often reaching a larger asymptotic mass of 4800 grams [Wwi = 4800 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is thought to be linked to male-male competition for territories and the physical demands of defending a nesting site. The maximum lifespan of this species, documented under the same thermal conditions typical of active metabolism at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], is approximately 36.6 years [am = approximately 36.6 years]. This impressive longevity is comparable to that of other large gruids and represents an extended period of reproductive potential that can compensate for the low annual fecundity. Field studies of marked individuals have revealed that survival rates remain high well into the third decade of life, with senescence becoming evident only after the age of thirty, when reproductive output begins to decline gradually.
